summary: Defines a way to classify the communication requirements of large-scale multicast applications, giving designers a shared vocabulary for comparing them. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Big group broadcasts come in many kinds. This sorts them into labeled boxes so people can talk about which one they need.

questions: what are large scale multicast application requirements
how do you classify multicast communication needs
what parameters describe a multicast application
subtitle: A classification system for communication needs of large-scale multicast applications.

tldr.problem: Large-scale multicast applications (video broadcasts, online games, financial data feeds) have wildly different communication requirements. No single protocol can satisfy all. Without a shared vocabulary, it is hard to compare what applications need or to design adaptive protocol frameworks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a taxonomy of communication parameters (reliability, ordering, timeliness, session control, topology, security, cost) with specific definitions, value types, and worst-case examples. Applications assign values to each parameter to describe their needs precisely, standardizing how requirements are stated.
tldr.outcome: Applications and protocol designers can now describe requirements consistently, identify worst-case scenarios, find where heterogeneity is highest, and match protocol mechanisms to application needs. This opens the door to dynamic protocol adaptation.

facts.label: Parameter categories
facts.value: Reliability, Ordering, Timeliness, Session Control, Topology, Directory, Security, Payment

facts.label: Worst-case examples
facts.value: Included for each parameter (video loss: 20%; audio jitter: <1ms; game late-join: not allowed)

facts.label: Scope levels
facts.value: Per stream, per session, per sender, per receiver

today: RFC 2729 introduced a taxonomy framework that influenced later thinking about application requirements in networking, though it was never standardized into a requirement-specification language. Modern approaches like software-defined networking and application-aware networking build on similar ideas of matching network behavior to application needs.

sections.title: Why a Taxonomy is Needed
sections.content:
Large-scale multicast applications span video broadcasts with thousands of viewers, multiplayer online games with tight latency budgets, financial data feeds that cannot lose updates, and many others. Each has different requirements for reliability (some can tolerate packet loss, others cannot), ordering (do packets need to arrive in order?), timeliness (how much latency is acceptable?), and security.

The challenge is that no single protocol can compromise between all these diverse requirements. Instead, systems need to identify which requirements matter most for a given application and select or adapt protocols accordingly. To do this reliably requires a standardized way for applications to state their needs. This taxonomy provides that shared vocabulary, organized into about ten categories of communication parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: When you order lunch, the restaurant needs to know: does it have to arrive in 10 minutes (pizza delivery) or 30 minutes (deli order)? Is it for one person or fifty? Does it need to be hot or is cold okay? Different answers change how the kitchen works.

sections.title: The Parameter Categories
sections.content: Reliability covers packet loss tolerance and component fault handling. Ordering specifies whether timing, sequencing, or causal ordering matters. Timeliness includes latency, jitter (variance in delay), hard versus soft real-time constraints, and burstiness of bandwidth. Session Control covers how sessions start, join/leave rules, and how many streams a session can have. Session Topology specifies numbers of senders and receivers. Directory covers how participants are discovered and mobility. Security includes authentication, tampering prevention, non-repudiation, denial-of-service resistance, and privacy. Security Dynamics covers compromise detection and recovery. Payment & Charging specifies cost models.
sections.plainLanguage: To describe a broadcast, you answer: Can people miss packets? Do updates need to be in order? How fast must data arrive? Can people join late? How many people? Do they need passwords? Do you bill per minute or per gigabyte?

sections.title: Reliability: Packet Loss and Fault Tolerance
sections.content:
Transactional reliability means all-or-nothing: either the entire transaction succeeds or it fails and is reported (like a bank transfer—both credit and debit must occur). Guaranteed delivery can be deferrable (retry until success) or immediate (fail if not delivered now). Tolerated loss is a fraction: video might tolerate 20% loss but stock quotes tolerate none. Semantic loss lets the application specify which frames may be dropped (video keyframes cannot, but intermediate frames can).

Component reliability covers fault handling: setup fail-over time (how long to switch to a backup), mean time between failures, and fail-over time during an active stream. Examples range from web servers (1-second fail-over) to audio conferences (indefinite MTBF expected).
sections.plainLanguage: Some things must arrive perfect (bank transfers). Some can skip (video frames). Some must arrive very fast (live chat). Some can wait a while (email). Engineers need to know which kind the application is.

sections.title: Timeliness: Latency, Jitter, and Ordering
sections.content:
Hard real-time means the system must guarantee timeliness or report failure before attempting the communication. Soft real-time allows statistical measures (95% probability of meeting the deadline). Synchronicity is the maximum time drift between multiple streams (audio and video must sync within 80ms for human perception). Jitter is variance in delay (audio streaming needs less than 1ms jitter).

Latency is time from initiation to result: audio conferences need 20ms, some process control needs near zero. Burstiness describes bandwidth variance: a video with chat has sudden bursts when clips are swapped; compressed audio has silence/talking variance.

Ordering can be by global timestamp, global sequence, per-sender sequence, or causal relationships. A game needs per-sender sequencing and global causality (shots must follow aiming), but not global timing.
sections.plainLanguage: Some apps need answers instantly (flight control). Some can wait (email). Some need multiple streams to stay in sync (video and audio lips). Some care about order (finance: credit before debit). Some are bursty (video calls with chat), others smooth.

sections.title: Session Control and Topology
sections.content:
Session Control defines how participants join: announcement (public multicast group), invitation (explicit list), or directive (forced). Rules specify whether late join is allowed, if temporary leave is allowed, and if late joiners can catch up (replay). Duration is specified as start time, end time, and active time (not counting breaks).

Session Topology is the number of senders and receivers, and how they relate. Some applications have one sender (broadcast), others are many-to-many (games). Atomic join means the session fails unless a quorum of participants accept the invitation. The taxonomy lists potential streams per session (a football broadcast might have 15 camera angles) versus active streams the application can consume (maybe only 6 at once).
sections.plainLanguage: Is it like an announcement everyone can join anytime (TV broadcast) or invitations to specific people (conference call)? Can people show up late? Can they take breaks? Can they see what they missed?

sections.title: Security and Costs
sections.content:
Security parameters are stated as the cost (in abstract currency) of mounting a successful attack. Authentication strength is the cost of hijacking a role (sender or receiver). Tamper-proofing is the cost of altering data, replaying data, or interfering with timeliness. Non-repudiation is the cost of faking an audit trail (proving something happened when it did not).

Additional security parameters include denial-of-service resistance, action restriction (role-based), privacy, confidentiality, retransmit prevention, membership criteria, and collusion prevention. Security Dynamics cover mean time between compromises and detection/recovery time limits. Payment & Charging specifies total cost, cost per time, and cost per megabyte.

The taxonomy notes that security is orthogonal: many non-security requirements can have a security requirement attached ("confidentiality of this parameter must cost more than $1 million to break").
sections.plainLanguage: How hard should it be to fake a message, steal credentials, or see private data? Who can send? Who can receive? How much will it cost to run?

references.text: Bagnall, P., Briscoe, B., and A. Poppitt, "Taxonomy of Communication Requirements for Large-scale Multicast Applications", RFC 2729, December 1999.
